title: When the sangha disappoints
hookLine: communities have flaws; stay kind, stay honest
tomorrow: how do you check a teacher before you trust one?

cards: Every group chat has the day it goes quiet after one message too many.
The Thursday sit group near Mai's program met tonight to plan the summer and had that day: two longtime members argued about moving the sit online, one walked out, and Mai sat there holding her tea.
Her text afterward was short: i thought Buddhists didn't fight. The texts would disagree with her.
They keep the record of a fight that split a whole community of monks, in the city of Kosambi, while the Buddha himself was there.

teach.b: It started small, a dispute over whether one monk had broken a rule. Then sides formed, and the monks wounded each other with words. The Buddha asked them to stop, and they told him, in effect, to stay out of it.
So he spoke verses on hatred and went off to stay alone in a forest.
One line, in Max Müller's translation of the Dhammapada: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love". And the story doesn't end there.

teach.h: THE VILLAGE STOPS FEEDING THE FIGHT.
teach.b: The lay people of Kosambi stopped bowing to the quarreling monks and stopped feeding them, until the monks made peace. That's the Buddhist answer.
The sangha is a refuge, and it's made of people, so the texts tell its fights honestly and give it ways back: admitting a fault out loud, forgiving, refusing to feed a grudge. Now a neighbor.

In the Torah, the commandment says "nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people", and Jewish teaching on Yom Kippur says that wrongs between people are mended only when you go to the person and set it right.
The shared part is real: don't carry a grudge inside your own community.
The difference is honest too. The Torah grounds it in God's command; the verse ends, I am the LORD. The Dhammapada grounds it in how hatred itself works, and calls that an old rule.

how: Buddhist monastic communities hold regular gatherings where monks and nuns admit faults to one another and settle disputes by set procedures; lay Buddhists recite the Dhammapada's verses on hatred and are taught to reconcile rather than nurse a grudge.

games.q: what does “when the sangha disappoints” mean?
o: a rule for expelling a monk who breaks a vow
the moment a temple closes its doors for good
what to do when your spiritual community lets you down

games.q: the quarrel and the way back — tap the pairs.
p: where the monks split into sides
told, in effect, to stay out of it
bear no grudge against your own people

s: the Buddhist texts show an early sangha that never fought
they record the quarrel at Kosambi, where the monks told the Buddha himself to stay out of it.
in the Kosambi story, lay people helped end the quarrel
they stopped bowing to and feeding the quarreling monks until the monks made peace.
the Dhammapada says hatred ends once the other side is beaten
in Max Müller's words: hatred ceases by love.

games.q: your family's temple has split over who controls the donations, and your aunt says she's done with all of them. what fits the Kosambi story?
o: fights are expected; stay kind, stay honest, and feed neither side's grudge.
leave: a sangha that fights has lost the right to be called a refuge.
pick the side that's right and help it win, so the fight ends sooner.
games.why: the texts record the sangha's fights honestly and the ways back. at Kosambi, the lay people stopped feeding the quarrel, and the monks made peace.

practice: Bring to mind one group you belong to that has let you down: a team, a family chat, a congregation. Say the line softly out loud, once: hatred does not cease by hatred.
Then sit and let that group come to mind as it is, flawed, and part of your life.

wordCard.voice: When the sangha disappoints: the day the community fails you, and the old ways back, admitting, forgiving, and letting the grudge go hungry.

orig.note: Pali: non-hatred, freedom from enmity; in the Dhammapada verse, the thing hatred ceases by.

carryVoice: Your line: flawed and dear. A grudge can't live long if nobody feeds it. Seventeen days of the block, kept.
